proofs.proof_tex:
All expectations, variances, probabilities, and convergence statements in this proof are taken under the row-specific randomization law.  The potential-outcome schedules are fixed, so assignment is the only source of randomness.

For \(1\le j\le B\), define
\[
Y_{Bj}:=X_{Bj}-\tau_{Bj},
\qquad
s_B:=\left(\sum_{j=1}^B\sigma_{Bj}^2\right)^{1/2}
=\sqrt{B V_B}.
\tag{1}
\]
The definitions \(\tau_{Bj}=\mathbb E X_{Bj}\) and \(\sigma_{Bj}^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_{Bj})\) imply
\[
\mathbb E Y_{Bj}=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y_{Bj})=\sigma_{Bj}^2.
\tag{2}
\]
Assumption~\texttt{ass:nondegenerate-average-variance} gives \(V_B\to V>0\).  Hence there is \(B_0\) such that
\[
V_B\ge V/2>0,
\qquad
s_B>0
\quad\text{for every }B\ge B_0.
\tag{3}
\]
Deleting the finitely many rows below \(B_0\) does not affect any asserted limit, so all normalizations below are made on this tail.

For each \(B\ge B_0\) and \(j\), let \(\mathsf D_{Bj}\) be the finite marginal design induced by \(X_{Bj}\) on its finite score support, and on that carrier define
\[
\widetilde Y_{Bj}:=\frac{Y_{Bj}}{s_B}.
\tag{4}
\]
Assumption~\texttt{ass:block-independence} says that the random pairs are mutually independent.  Their score-coordinate projections are therefore mutually independent, so the joint row law of \((X_{B1},\ldots,X_{BB})\) is the product of the marginal designs \((\mathsf D_{B1},\ldots,\mathsf D_{BB})\).  By (2),
\[
\mathbb E_{\mathsf D_{Bj}}\widetilde Y_{Bj}=0.
\tag{5}
\]
For distinct \(j,k\), product factorization and (5) give
\[
\mathbb E(\widetilde Y_{Bj}\widetilde Y_{Bk})
=\mathbb E\widetilde Y_{Bj}\,\mathbb E\widetilde Y_{Bk}=0.
\tag{6}
\]
Consequently, expanding the square and using (1), (2), and (5)--(6) yields the exact product-design normalization
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^B\widetilde Y_{Bj}\right)
&=\sum_{j=1}^B\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde Y_{Bj})
+2\sum_{1\le j<k\le B}\operatorname{Cov}(\widetilde Y_{Bj},\widetilde Y_{Bk})\\
&=\frac{1}{s_B^2}\sum_{j=1}^B\sigma_{Bj}^2=1.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]

Assumption~\texttt{ass:uniform-score-bound} and the inequality \(|\mathbb E X_{Bj}|\le\mathbb E|X_{Bj}|\) give
\[
|\tau_{Bj}|\le M,
\qquad
|\widetilde Y_{Bj}|
\le\delta_B:=\frac{2M}{s_B}.
\tag{8}
\]
Equations (1) and (3) show both envelope conditions
\[
0\le\delta_B\longrightarrow0,
\qquad
B\delta_B^3
=\frac{8M^3B}{(B V_B)^{3/2}}
=\frac{8M^3}{\sqrt B\,V_B^{3/2}}
\longrightarrow0.
\tag{9}
\]
Apply \texttt{Causalean.Experimentation.DesignBased.prodDesign\_clt} to the tail array with coordinate set \(\{1,\ldots,B\}\), marginal designs \(\mathsf D_{Bj}\), summands \(\widetilde Y_{Bj}\), and envelope \(\delta_B\).  Its mean-zero, unit-variance, vanishing-envelope, and cardinality-times-cubed-envelope hypotheses are respectively (5), (7), and (8)--(9).  The theorem therefore gives, for every \(t\in\mathbb R\),
\[
\Pr\!\left\{\sum_{j=1}^B\widetilde Y_{Bj}\le t\right\}
\longrightarrow\Phi(t).
\tag{10}
\]
The product-law identity from Assumption~\texttt{ass:block-independence} transfers this conclusion from the product design to the stated row randomization law.  By the definitions of \(\widehat\tau_B\), \(\bar\tau_B\), and (1),
\[
T_B:=\frac{\sqrt B(\widehat\tau_B-\bar\tau_B)}{\sqrt{V_B}}
=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^B(X_{Bj}-\tau_{Bj})}{\sqrt{B V_B}}
=\sum_{j=1}^B\widetilde Y_{Bj}.
\tag{11}
\]
Thus (10)--(11) prove \(T_B\Rightarrow N(0,1)\) from the primitive design conditions.

We next derive, rather than assume, the denominator law.  Set
\[
D_B:=\widehat W_B-W_B
=\frac1B\sum_{j=1}^B(G_{Bj}-b_{Bj}).
\tag{12}
\]
The definition \(b_{Bj}=\mathbb E G_{Bj}\) gives \(\mathbb E D_B=0\).  Assumption~\texttt{ass:block-independence} makes the variables \(G_{B1},\ldots,G_{BB}\) independent because they are coordinate projections of independent pairs.  Hence their cross-block covariances vanish, and Assumption~\texttt{ass:bound-lln} gives
\[
\mathbb E D_B^2
=\operatorname{Var}(D_B)
=\frac1{B^2}\sum_{j=1}^B\operatorname{Var}(G_{Bj})
\longrightarrow0.
\tag{13}
\]
For every \(\varepsilon>0\), the pointwise inequality
\[
\varepsilon^2\mathbf 1\{|D_B|>\varepsilon\}\le D_B^2
\tag{14}
\]
and (13) imply the Chebyshev bound
\[
\Pr(|\widehat W_B-W_B|>\varepsilon)
\le\frac{\mathbb E D_B^2}{\varepsilon^2}
\longrightarrow0.
\tag{15}
\]
Therefore \(\widehat W_B-W_B\xrightarrow{p}0\).  A simple sufficient condition for Assumption~\texttt{ass:bound-lln} is the existence of \(C<\infty\) such that
\[
\sup_{B\ge1}\max_{1\le j\le B}
\mathbb E[(G_{Bj}-b_{Bj})^2]\le C,
\tag{16}
\]
because the right-hand side of (13) is then at most \(C/B\).  In particular, if every finite lookup table is uniformly bounded by \(|G_{Bj}|\le L<\infty\), then \(|b_{Bj}|\le L\), the left-hand side of (16) is at most \(4L^2\), and (16) holds.  Mere finiteness of each row supplies neither a common \(L\) nor (13).

Assumption~\texttt{ass:block-conservativeness} and the definitions of \(W_B\) and \(V_B\) imply
\[
W_B-V_B
=\frac1B\sum_{j=1}^B(b_{Bj}-\sigma_{Bj}^2)\ge0.
\tag{17}
\]
For \(B\ge B_0\), define
\[
R_B:=\frac{\max(\widehat W_B,0)}{V_B}.
\tag{18}
\]
The division is valid by (3).  Fix \(\eta\in(0,1)\).  Since \(\max(\widehat W_B,0)\ge\widehat W_B\), the event \(R_B<1-\eta\), together with (17), implies \(W_B-\widehat W_B>\eta V_B\).  Thus (3) and (15) give
\[
\Pr(R_B<1-\eta)
\le\Pr(|\widehat W_B-W_B|>\eta V_B)
\le\Pr(|\widehat W_B-W_B|>\eta V/2)
\longrightarrow0.
\tag{19}
\]

Definition~\texttt{def:wald-interval} and (11), (18) give the exact event identity
\[
\{\bar\tau_B\in I_B(\alpha)\}
=\{|T_B|\le z_\alpha\sqrt{R_B}\}.
\tag{20}
\]
Because \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), one has \(z_\alpha=\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/2)>0\).  On \(\{R_B\ge1-\eta\}\), the event \(\{|T_B|\le z_\alpha\sqrt{1-\eta}\}\) is contained in the event in (20).  Therefore (10)--(11), (19), and the absence of atoms in the standard normal law imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
\liminf_{B\to\infty}\Pr\{\bar\tau_B\in I_B(\alpha)\}
&\ge \lim_{B\to\infty}
\Pr\{|T_B|\le z_\alpha\sqrt{1-\eta}\}\\
&=2\Phi\!\left(z_\alpha\sqrt{1-\eta}\right)-1.
\end{aligned}
\tag{21}
\]
Letting \(\eta\downarrow0\), continuity of \(\Phi\) and the definition of \(z_\alpha\) yield
\[
\liminf_{B\to\infty}\Pr\{\bar\tau_B\in I_B(\alpha)\}
\ge2\Phi(z_\alpha)-1=1-\alpha.
\tag{22}
\]

Suppose now that \(W_B\to W<\infty\).  Equation (17) and \(V_B\to V\) imply \(W\ge V>0\).  Equation (15) then gives \(\widehat W_B\xrightarrow{p}W\); continuity of truncation and division by \(V_B\to V>0\) gives
\[
R_B\xrightarrow{p}r:=W/V\ge1.
\tag{23}
\]
For any \(\delta\in(0,r)\), the event \(r-\delta\le R_B\le r+\delta\) has probability tending to one.  Hence
\[
\Pr\{|T_B|\le z_\alpha\sqrt{r-\delta}\}-o(1)
\le\Pr\{\bar\tau_B\in I_B(\alpha)\}
\le\Pr\{|T_B|\le z_\alpha\sqrt{r+\delta}\}+o(1).
\tag{24}
\]
Using (10)--(11) at the two fixed thresholds and then letting \(\delta\downarrow0\) proves
\[
\Pr\{\bar\tau_B\in I_B(\alpha)\}
\longrightarrow
2\Phi\!\left(z_\alpha\sqrt{W/V}\right)-1.
\tag{25}
\]

Finally, suppose \(W_B-V_B\to0\).  Equations (3), (15), and this condition imply
\[
\frac{\widehat W_B}{V_B}-1
=\frac{\widehat W_B-W_B}{V_B}
+\frac{W_B-V_B}{V_B}
\xrightarrow{p}0,
\qquad
R_B\xrightarrow{p}1.
\tag{26}
\]
In particular, \(\Pr(\widehat W_B>0)\to1\).  Define the feasible statistic on that event by
\[
U_B:=\frac{\sqrt B(\widehat\tau_B-\bar\tau_B)}
{\sqrt{\max(\widehat W_B,0)}}
=\frac{T_B}{\sqrt{R_B}},
\tag{27}
\]
and assign it any fixed value when its denominator is zero.  By (26), \(R_B^{-1/2}\xrightarrow{p}1\) on an event whose probability tends to one; by (10)--(11), \(T_B\) is tight.  Hence, for \(L>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
\Pr(|U_B-T_B|>\varepsilon)
\le \Pr(|T_B|>L)
+\Pr\{R_B>0,\ |R_B^{-1/2}-1|>\varepsilon/L\}
+\Pr(R_B=0).
\tag{28}
\]
First choose \(L\) large by tightness and then use (26); this proves \(U_B-T_B\xrightarrow{p}0\).  For every \(x\in\mathbb R\) and \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
\Pr(T_B\le x-\varepsilon)-\Pr(|U_B-T_B|>\varepsilon)
\le\Pr(U_B\le x)
\le\Pr(T_B\le x+\varepsilon)+\Pr(|U_B-T_B|>\varepsilon).
\tag{29}
\]
Apply (10)--(11) and then let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\); continuity of \(\Phi\) proves \(U_B\Rightarrow N(0,1)\).

To stress-test the scope, fix \(\alpha\in(0,1)\).  Since \(z_\alpha>0\), density of the rationals gives \(\rho\in\mathbb Q\) with
\[
0<\rho<\min\{z_\alpha^2,1-\alpha\}.
\tag{30}
\]
Consider the four assignment atoms \(z=(x,h)\in\{-1,1\}\times\{0,1\}\), with
\[
p_{(x,h)}=\frac12\rho^h(1-\rho)^{1-h}.
\tag{31}
\]
These probabilities are positive and rational.  Take the one-coordinate binary schedule \(\theta_0=1\), reveal \(O_z=\{0\}\) at every atom, set \(v_{(x,h),0}=x\), and use the observable assignment table \(G_{(x,h)}=h/\rho\).  Then
\[
X_{(x,h)}=x,
\qquad
c=\mathbb E X=0,
\qquad
\tau(\theta)=c\theta_0=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X)=1=\mathbb E G.
\tag{32}
\]
The expected rule is in fact conservative on the entire binary schedule space: its expectation is one, whereas the score variance is zero at \(\theta_0=0\) and one at \(\theta_0=1\).  At the displayed schedule, expected conservativeness holds with equality.  For \(B=1\), when \(h=0\) the interval radius is zero and its center \(x\in\{-1,1\}\) excludes zero; when \(h=1\), its radius is \(z_\alpha/\sqrt\rho>1\) and it contains zero.  Exact enumeration of the four atoms therefore gives coverage
\[
\Pr\{0\in I_1(\alpha)\}=\Pr(h=1)=\rho<1-\alpha.
\tag{33}
\]
Under independent replication of this fixed block, \(|X|\le1\), \(V_B=1\), \(b_{Bj}=\sigma_{Bj}^2=1\), and
\[
\frac1{B^2}\sum_{j=1}^B\operatorname{Var}(G_{Bj})
=\frac{\rho^{-1}-1}{B}\longrightarrow0.
\tag{34}
\]
Thus the finite-sample failure is compatible with every asymptotic primitive used above.  It confirms that (22) is an asymptotic coverage statement and cannot be strengthened here to finite-sample coverage. \(\square\)

prose_updates.tldr: A six-coordinate three-atom experiment has all-observable variance-bound optimum \(107/72\), full Boolean quadratic/cubic optimum \(55/36\), and direct Harshaw--Middleton--Savje positive-semidefinite quadratic optimum \(7/6+\sqrt{17}/9\). Thus the exact quartic gaps are respectively \(1/24\) against every observable Boolean quadratic or cubic rule and \((8\sqrt{17}-23)/72\) against the published quadratic class. The quartic optimizer has an assignmentwise nonnegative rational implementation. More generally, for fixed binary potential outcomes under a finite known randomization, expected observed-data rules are exactly the Boolean Mobius span generated by jointly observable subsets, universal conservativeness is finite pointwise domination, and the observable-margin dual characterizes the Pareto-admissible class. Complement symmetry explains the quartic threshold, and independent replication preserves the block gap. For independent triangular arrays, the formally verified finite-design product central limit theorem applies after deriving its unit-variance and vanishing-envelope premises from block independence, bounded scores, and nondegenerate average variance; the primitive condition \(B^{-2}\sum_j\operatorname{Var}(G_{Bj})\to0\) separately yields the denominator law and asymptotically conservative studentized coverage.

project_justification.fill: The project gives exact certificates for the all-observable value \(107/72\), the Boolean degree-at-most-three value \(55/36\), and the Harshaw--Middleton--Savje semidefinite value \(7/6+\sqrt{17}/9\). It combines these with the if-and-only-if Boolean support theorem, finite pointwise conservative cone, observable-margin dual, Pareto complete class, rational-certificate corollary, nonnegative implementation, and an exact product law whose degree-restricted part is certified by its own finite linear-program dual. For independent triangular arrays, centering and normalization reduce the numerator directly to the formally verified Causalean finite-design product central limit theorem: block independence gives the product law and unit variance, while bounded scores and \(V_B\to V>0\) give the two envelope limits. The primitive row-average variance condition on the realized bound tables then yields the denominator weak law by Chebyshev's inequality and licenses conservative Wald coverage.

sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: None in the finite characterization. In the triangular-array inference result, assignment is still the only source of randomness. Block independence, bounded scores, and \(V_B\to V>0\) verify the product-design central limit theorem's normalization and envelope hypotheses. Independently, \(B^{-2}\sum_j\operatorname{Var}(G_{Bj})\to0\) yields \(\widehat W_B-W_B\xrightarrow{p}0\); a uniform centered second-moment bound gives the explicit upper bound \(C/B\).

prose_updates.related_work: \cite{HarshawMiddletonSavje2026}, especially Proposition 1, Theorems 1 and 3, Definitions 1--2, and Section 8, supplies the quadratic characterization and supporting-objective theory and explicitly restricts attention to quadratic bounds. Its pairwise design-compatibility criterion embeds every published candidate into the Boolean quadratic cone, while its positive-semidefinite domination requirement makes that class strictly smaller than cube-wise Boolean domination. For the six-coordinate witness, the present exact rank-one primal and algebraic dual-slack certificate solves the published semidefinite program itself at \(7/6+\sqrt{17}/9\), not merely at the containing Boolean lower bound \(55/36\). The resulting direct gap from the quartic optimum is \((8\sqrt{17}-23)/72\). The Harshaw--Middleton--Savje use of \cite{PaluckShepherdAronow2016} is a quadratic school-data empirical illustration, not a reanalysis of the original causal conclusions. \cite{Middleton2021Unifying}, \emph{Unifying Design-based Inference: On Bounding and Estimating the Variance of any Linear Estimator in any Experimental Design}, supplies the arbitrary design--estimator--bound triplet but remains matrix-quadratic. Proposition 2 and Corollary 2 of \cite{AronowSamii2013} use Young's inequality to construct a weakly conservative Horvitz--Thompson correction when pairwise inclusion probabilities vanish; its binary restriction lies in \(\mathcal C_{\mathcal J}(f)\cap\mathcal E_{\mathcal J,2}\), but that paper does not characterize the full Boolean observable-margin cone, its Pareto complete class, or the strict quartic separation. \cite{Lu2019FactorialBinary} supplies a sharp binary inclusion--exclusion correction for the \(2^2\) factorial design, while \cite{AronowGreenLee2014} supplies sharp marginal variance bounds for difference-in-means under complete randomization. \cite{ChattopadhyayImbens2025} develops imputation and contrast variance estimators, including nonquadratic procedures, but does not characterize the complete observable-function space or its Pareto frontier. \cite{AronowSamii2017Interference} fixes the design--exposure--estimand semantics and supplies inverse-probability variance estimation and local-dependence asymptotics for the school-network consumer. \cite{LiDing2017FPCLT} supplies the finite-population limit-theory benchmark. The supporting inference theorem here instead discharges its numerator limit by direct reuse of the formally verified Causalean finite-design product central limit theorem after proving that the normalized independent blocks satisfy its unit-variance and envelope premises; it derives the denominator weak law by Chebyshev's inequality from \(B^{-2}\sum_j\operatorname{Var}(G_{Bj})\to0\), with blockwise conservativeness kept as a distinct premise. \cite{AzrielKriegerKapelner2026}, \emph{Optimal Designs with Robust Inference for Binary Treatment Effects}, studies balanced designs and conservative CMH- and Robins-type inference under random binary potential outcomes, not unrestricted fixed binary schedules under a fixed arbitrary design.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: Exact enumeration uses \(2^K\) domination inequalities, \(|\mathcal J|\) coefficients, and assignment truth tables of total size \(\sum_z2^{|O_z|}\). Independent product designs tensorize exactly, but this gives no lossless decomposition for a large connected school network. Nonnegative expected bounds also need not admit nonnegative assignmentwise tables, although the displayed quartic witness does. Finiteness of every row does not by itself give a triangular-array denominator law: the inference result requires \(B^{-2}\sum_j\operatorname{Var}(G_{Bj})\to0\); uniformly bounded lookup tables are a simple sufficient condition, but rare observation probabilities can destroy uniform boundedness. The numerator proof is specific to independent product rows; it does not establish a central limit theorem for connected dependent-exposure arrays. If \(q\) is not complement invariant, averaging a bound with its complemented version can change the objective; the odd-degree collapse then supplies no degree-three limitation, and no unsymmetric cubic-equals-quadratic claim is made.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The exact \(107/72\), \(55/36\), and \(7/6+\sqrt{17}/9\) witness values have finite or algebraic certificates; the school-network exposure-block question remains open. The complete observable-function and Pareto results concern fixed binary schedules and finite randomized designs with arbitrary real probabilities on their support; rationality is required only for exact rational optimizer and assignment-table certificates and for the displayed witness. The binary Aronow--Samii specialization records a published conservative Horvitz--Thompson baseline and is not claimed as a new correction. There is no finite-sample coverage claim, no universal interval-shortening claim, no efficient general large-design algorithm, and no extension to real outcomes. Conservative studentized coverage is an asymptotic independent-block result. Its numerator central limit theorem follows by direct application of the formally verified finite-design product theorem after block independence, bounded scores, and \(V_B\to V>0\) establish the product law, exact normalization, and vanishing-envelope conditions. Its denominator weak law follows separately from \(B^{-2}\sum_j\operatorname{Var}(G_{Bj})\to0\); uniformly bounded finite lookup tables are sufficient but are not automatic across a triangular array. A four-atom binary experiment satisfies all replicated asymptotic primitives while failing nominal coverage at \(B=1\), so no finite-sample inference conclusion is implicit. The direct Harshaw--Middleton--Savje calculation is an exact six-dimensional witness semidefinite program, not a consumer-scale computation. Under full joint observability the theory reduces to exact variance estimability; under the stated complement symmetries and observation sets of size at most three it reduces to quadratic optimality, while no odd-degree collapse is claimed for asymmetric objective weights. The Harshaw--Middleton--Savje school-data analysis is only a quadratic empirical illustration, not a reanalysis of the original causal conclusions.

statement_notes.justification: Expected conservativeness alone does not imply coverage. The theorem derives the numerator central limit theorem from primitive independent-block conditions through the formally verified finite-design product result, derives the denominator weak law from the row-average variance condition, and uses the correctly scaled \(B^{-1/2}\) standard error.
statement_notes.gap: \cite{LiDing2017FPCLT} supplies a finite-population central-limit benchmark and \cite{HarshawMiddletonSavje2026} supplies quadratic bound-estimator consistency conditions, but neither composes an all-degree observable bound with the direct finite-design product theorem, a derived lookup-table weak law, and conservative studentization.
statement_notes.consumer: It licenses asymptotic Wald inference for genuinely independent replicated binary exposure blocks using realized higher-order lookup tables whose row-average design variance is negligible; it does not license connected-network or finite-sample inference.
